text: The Canaanites lived in the land of Canaan, in a region called the Levant.
More than 4,000 years ago, clay tablets at Ebla already listed gifts for their gods El, Baal and Dagon.
src: the peoples of the land of Canaan in the southern Levant
The earliest evidence comes from the Ebla tablets / dated to the second half of the 3rd millennium BCE, which list offerings to the chief Canaanite gods El, Baal and Dagon

text: The Canaanites honoured many gods, led by El and his wife Asherah.
Baal was the storm god who brought the rain.
src: The Canaanites honoured a pantheon headed by El and his consort Asherah
Baal Hadad, the storm god who brought the rain

text: Most of what is known comes from clay tablets found at Ugarit and from carved stones like the Mesha Stele.
One story tells how Baal was swallowed by Death and a drought followed, until he came back with the rain.
src: Most of what is known comes from the clay tablets of Ugarit / the Mesha Stele of Moab
Baal is swallowed by Mot, Death, and a terrible drought follows / Baal returns with the rain

text: People worshipped on hilltops, called “high places”, among trees and standing stones.
Families honoured their dead with food, drink, incense and music.
src: often on hilltops or “high places” among groves of trees, with standing stones or pillars
dead relatives were venerated / given food and drink / with incense, libations, music and devotional songs

text: Each city had its own god, such as Eshmun of Sidon.
Phoenician sailors carried the religion west, to Carthage in North Africa.
src: peoples and cities formed regional and national cults round a patron god / Eshmun of Sidon
Carried west by Phoenician sailors / Phoenicians founded Carthage and other Punic communities in North Africa

text: Its last worship died out more than 1,600 years ago.
Traces of it live on in Greek myths and in the names of places.
src: survived in some places until the 4th century CE / The last Punic religious practices die out
Canaanite ideas can be seen in Greek mythology / Words and places kept its traces too
